paragraphs.source_en: Unlike the paintings of the Pastoral style which is widespread across the Central Sahara, the distribution of the Round Heads outside the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart, Acacus and the Djado mountains is questionable. Possible Round Head paintings were reported as far away as in the Jebel Uweinat, on the border between Libya, Egypt and Sudan (Zboray 2006) and also in the Ennedi massif (Jelinek 2004). In such distant regions, the main criteria for the attribution of the paintings to the Round Head art, has traditionally been the similarity of their anthropomorphic figures, and particularly the circular shape of the heads. However, more criteria should be applied to point out the similarities and diversities of various painted complexes.

paragraphs.source_en: The rock art research in the massifs outside the area of the Round Head distribution has been mainly concentrated on large engravings of wild and domesticated animals and on Pastoral paintings. Small paintings and engravings of anthropomorphic figures resembling the Kel Essuf images have not been reported except in a few rare cases (Hallier & Hallier 1999), contributing to a serious lack of information concerning the earliest forms of the rock art. Not only has attention not been paid to the "non-attractive" small-sized rock art, but also entire regions have not been explored, mainly because of the difficult political situation in the Niger, Chad and Sudan, which makes access to these sites difficult.

paragraphs.source_en: The consequence of this imbalance is that the majority of documentation in the Hoggar, Air, Adrar Bous, Tibesti and Ennedi, consists of Bubaline engravings, Pastoral engravings and paintings and post-Neolithic rock art. The situation is further complicated by an absence of direct dating for the early rock art, and so even if there are similarities between the paintings in the neighbouring regions, they may be of a different period.

paragraphs.source_en: Simple anthropomorphic figures resembling Kel Essuf engravings and presumed early forms of Round Heads were documented in the northern and southern Tibesti (Hallier & Hallier 1999). The images consist of an oval body with short arms and legs, represented frontally in a static position. Although the region is near the Djado and the Algerian Tadrart, such extremely simple forms can be actually found anywhere in the world. The same applies for elementary engraved motifs such as circles, concentric circles, ovals, spirals and lines, which are present in virtually the whole of Africa and it is therefore impossible to attribute them to a single culture or demonstrate any contact between the groups.
